targetText: As soon as society is in possession of all means of production the duty of all able-bodied people, irrespective of sex, to work becomes the basic law of socialised society.
summary: In the first chapter of 'The Socialisation of Society', Bebel outlines the fundamental laws of socialist society: the universal duty of all able-bodied persons to work, democratic workplace administration, the replacement of money and commodity trade with labor certificates, and the drastic reduction of the working day through advanced technology and the abolition of parasitic labor.

targetText: A need deeply implanted in human nature is to be free to choose an occupation and to change it at will. Just as constant repetition makes the choicest dish repulsive, so does the treadmill of a repetitive occupation day in day out render the mind dull and slack. Man works only mechanically, does what he has to do without any higher inspiration and enjoyment. In every man there are latent abilities and inclinations which only need to be awakened and developed to produce the most beautiful results. Only then will man become full man.
summary: Human nature and the division of labour: varied activity unlocks all-round human potential under socialism.
explanation: Bebel argues that human nature naturally craves variety and freedom of choice, which capitalist lifelong division of labour deadens through mechanical repetition. By drastically reducing working hours and eliminating class specialization, socialist society enables every person to awaken their latent abilities across multiple fields.
context: Section 2: Harmonious Development of Mental and Physical Labour
